Abstract
Estimating Body Mass Index (BMI) from camera images
facilitates rapid weight assessment in situations where tradi-
tional measurement methods are impractical or inaccessible,
such as telehealth services and emergency medical scenarios.
Recent computer vision-based approaches for BMI estima-
tion have predominantly been limited to datasets of up to
7,211 full-body images or 14,500 facial images. In this study,
we present a comprehensive evaluation of BMI estimation
from smartphone camera images using deep learning on a
significantly larger, proprietary, real-world dataset compris-
ing 84,963 images collected from 25,353 individuals. We
introduce an automatic image filtering strategy based on
posture clustering and person detection to effectively curate
the real-world dataset, ensuring the exclusion of unsuitable
images, such as those with atypical postures or incomplete
views of the body. We achieve a Mean Absolute Percentage
Error (MAPE) of 8% on our hold-out test dataset (real-world
data only), using full-torso images. Further, when training
solely on the real-world dataset and evaluating on the com-
pletely unseen Visual-Body-To-BMI dataset, we achieve an
MAPE of 13%, comparable with state-of-the-art approaches
trained on Visual-Body-To-BMI, demonstrating robust gen-
eralization. We also evaluate our model’s generalizability on
two additional external benchmark datasets: the full-body
Celeb-FBI dataset and the face-only VIP-Attribute dataset,
achieving an MAPE of 23.64 % and 25.21 % respectively.
Moreover, we analyze the impact of image perspective on
BMI estimation performance within our real-world dataset,
comparing full-body, torso-up, and face-only images. Our
results indicate that torso-up images deliver performance
similar to full-body images (9% MAPE), while face-only
images yield comparatively lower accuracy (11% MAPE).
We demonstrate the real-world applicability of our BMI es-
timation approach by deploying our algorithms for image
filtering and BMI estimation, implemented in Python, di-
rectly on mobile devices using the CLAID framework. We
report the processing speed for filtering and inference on
Android and iOS devices. We provide the code for training,
deployment, and the mobile applications, as open-source
contributions.
1. Introduction
A high Body Mass Index (BMI) is associated with various
chronic diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, certain
types of cancer, and metabolic disorders such as diabetes [1].
Body weight and weight changes are essential indicators of
health and disease risk. For overweight individuals, a body

weight loss of 5% can lead to significant improvements in
health outcomes, such as the prevention of type 2 diabetes
and cardiovascular diseases [2]. Traditionally, the calculation
of BMI requires measuring a person’s weight and height us-
ing scales and a stadiometer. In medical emergencies, there
is a well-documented need for faster weight estimation meth-
ods [3, 4]. In such situations, the patient’s own estimate of
body weight remains the most accurate assessment, but in
situations where the patient is unresponsive, confused, or
otherwise unable to provide an estimate, alternative meth-
ods are needed. Body weight estimation from smartphone
camera images offers a digital, real-time capable solution.
By analyzing images of individuals, deep-learning models
can estimate body weight without the direct participation
of individuals. BMI estimation from images alone can be
particularly useful in remote health monitoring when direct
measurements of height and weight are not possible. Past
studies have explored the use of deep learning models to
estimate body weight from images with promising results.
Jin et al. (2022) [5] show state-of-the-art results, achieving a
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 9.37% when
estimating BMI from full-body images. Other studies have
explored weight estimation using only facial images [6, 7],
achieving a Mean Absolute Error of 2,3.
However, many past studies have been limited by small
datasets, containing only up to 5,900 images[8]. The limited
dataset size may restrict the model’s ability to learn complex
patterns and generalize to diverse body types. Further, sep-
arate studies have explored different perspectives for BMI
estimation, such as full-body [5, 8, 9], and face-only im-
ages [6, 7]. Due to the heterogeneity of the datasets used in
these studies, we currently lack a systematic comparison of
different image perspectives for weight estimation.
To address the gap in datasets of limited size, we train
deep learning models on a large-scale, real-world dataset
of over 84,000 full-body images of 25,353 individuals. We
evaluate the performance on the Visua-body-to-BMI [8],
Celebi-FBI[9] and VIP-Attribute dataset[7], and compare
our results with existing state-of-the-art methods. To address
the gap of limited evaluation across different image perspec-
tives from the same individuals, we conduct a comparative
analysis of weight estimation performance across three dif-
ferent image perspectives: full-body, torso-up, and face-only.
We aim to uncover how various views of the body influ-
ence the accuracy of weight predictions, providing insights
into the most effective approaches for different application
scenarios. The remainder of the work is structured as fol-
lows: Section 2 provides an overview of related work in the
field of weight estimation from images. Section 3 details
our methodology, including the dataset, model architecture,
and filtering approach. Section 4 presents the experimental
results of our model on the internal and external datasets.
Section 5 concludes with a discussion of the results and
limitations.
2. Related Work
Prior research has explored various approaches to estimating
body weight and BMI using machine learning methods ap-
plied to images captured from different perspectives. Early
work focused on facial images [15, 17], while more recent
studies have also explored full-body images [10, 8, 5, 14, 9]
and smartphone camera images [12, 13]. Various target vari-
ables have been used in the literature, including body mass
index [11, 5, 14, 9], body weight [12, 15, 6], and body fat
metrics [13, 12]. Table 1 provides a selected overview of
related work on body weight estimation from images, includ-
ing the dataset used and the estimation performance.
Datasets
Prior research has employed annotated images
from a variety of datasets with differing sizes and character-
istics. For full-body images, dataset sizes range from around
150 subjects [12, 13, 11] to nearly 6000 subjects [8]. For
facial images, dataset sizes range from 50 individuals [17] to
14,500 images [15]. Various authors have proposed public
benchmark datasets for body weight and BMI estimation,
such as the Visual-Body-To-BMI dataset [8] and the Celeb-
FBI dataset [9], both containing full-body images sourced
from social media and celebrities, respectively. The VIP-
attribute dataset [7] proposes a benchmark dataset for facial
images, containing images of 1026 celebrities.
Existing machine learning approaches
Some early ap-
proaches for BMI estimation from images relied on manually
engineered features to extract meaningful information before
training computational models. Examples include extracting
body keypoints [8, 10], facial landmarks [17], and silhouette
masks capturing body contours [11]. Such features were used
as input to machine learning models, such as SVM regres-
sions [15, 8] or random forests [17]. More recent work has
adopted deep learning models to learn features directly from
the images [5, 7, 6]. Various CNN architectures have been
explored, such as ResNet [6, 7] and VGG [9, 11]. Jin et al.
(2022) [5] compared the performance of various CNN archi-
tectures on the Visual-Body-To-BMI [8] dataset, identifying
a Densenet architecture as the strong model, outperforming
similarly sized ResNet and VGG models. Their work also
introduced an attention mechanism to prioritize the most
informative regions of an image, improving the model’s per-
formance.
Full-body and face-only perspectives
Various perspec-
tives of images suitable for BMI estimation have been ex-
plored in prior work. The primary distinction has been made
between full-body images and facial images. For the task of
BMI estimation, past work has achieved an MAE of 3.03 on

the Visual-Body-To-BMI dataset [8] using full-body images
[5]. Facial images from different datasets have also been
used for BMI estimation, achieving an MAE of 2.3 on the
VIP-attribute dataset [7]. Additionally, for full-body images,
work by Kim et al. (2023) [14] explored the impact of com-
bining three different perspectives (front, side, and back) in
a single model on the task of BMI estimation, achieving a
BMI prediction MAE of 3.12 on their own dataset. Further,
a study by Farina et al. [13] investigated the use of side-
view smartphone images for body fat estimation, achieving
a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.11 kg on a dataset of 158
images.
Image filtering techniques
To ensure models are trained
on high-quality and relevant images, some previous studies
have implemented filtering processes to exclude unsuitable
or outlier images, such as those with distorted shapes or im-
proper perspective. Majmudar et al.(2022) and Debnath et al.
(2024) describe manually removing images of poor quality
[12, 9]. In contrast, other authors have applied automated
filtering processes based on the presence of required body

3. Methodology
In this section, we describe our approach to estimating BMI
of a person from real-world smartphone camera images. First,
we describe the filtering process we employ to remove un-
suitable images from the real-world dataset (cf. Section3.1).
We further describe cropping strategies to obtain different
image perspectives, i.e., full body, torso-up, and face-only
images (cf. Section 3.2). Lastly, we explain the implementa-
tion and training of the deep learning model used for BMI
estimation (cf. Section 3.3).
3.1. Image filtering
Images captured in real-life scenarios often exhibit signifi-
cant variation in factors such as image quality, lighting, and
subject posture. Some images - particularly those taken from
uncommon angles or with atypical postures - may be unsuit-
able for accurate BMI estimation. To ensure that we only
include suitable images into our dataset, we apply a filtering
process to automatically curate the real-world dataset. Our
goal is to remove images that do not (clearly) contain a hu-
man body, images with a camera angle that is too low or too
high (such as selfies), and images with outlying postures.
To identify outlier images, we apply a set of filtering steps
based on human bounding box and body keypoint data, both
obtained using the Detectron2 framework [18]. The Detec-
tron2 framework provides models for human bounding box
estimation, including confidence scores, as well as skeleton
estimation with 17 human body keypoints. Using bounding
pox and keypoint estimations, we apply three filtering steps:
1. Person detection: Images with a human bounding box
confidence score of less than a certain threshold are re-
moved
2. Person-to-background-ratio: Images with a bounding-
box-to-image-area-ratio below a certain threshold are
removed (see Figure 5 in the results for an example)
3. Posture clustering: images with outlying combinations of
body keypoints were clustered and removed (details in
the below subsection)
Each filtering step is applied independently, and the images
that meet any of the conditions are removed from the dataset.
We note, that it is possible for one image to meet multiple
filtering conditions at once.
Posture clustering
Participants received instructions to have another person
take their picture from a distance in a front-facing, full-
body position. Visual inspection of our dataset confirms that
most participants followed these instructions and maintained
suitable postures. Given that most people uploaded good
pictures, we apply k-means clustering to the extracted pose
keypoints to distinguish suitable postures from outliers. This
clustering allows us to filter out images where the subject
displays unsuitable poses - such as twisted arms or legs -or
where the photo was taken from an elevated angle, such as
selfies.
To ensures that the clustering is based on the relative po-
sition of the keypoints rather than the absolute position (i.e.,
given different sizes and positions of each person in the pic-
ture), we normalize the coordinates of the body keypoints by
dividing them by the individual image width and height. This
also allows us the plot the keypoints on a common scale for
visual inspection. For each image, we have a set of 34 nor-
malized coordinates (17 keypoints with x and y coordinates).
Since not all keypoints provide discriminative information,
we apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce
the dimensionality of the data. We remove components as
many as long as we retain 95% of the variance in the data.
We then apply K-means clustering to the dimensionality-
reduced dataset of keypoint coordinates. We evaluate k=1
to k=10 clusters. Using the elbow method, we determine
the optimal number of clusters. Afterwards, using visual in-
spection, we determine which clusters correspond to useable
poses. The other clusters are removed from the dataset.
3.2. Perspective cropping
We consider three perspectives: full-body, torso-up, and face-
only. The full-body perspective contains the entire body of
the individual, the torso-up perspective contains the body
from the shoulders up, and the face-only perspective contains
only the face of the individual. We obtain the torso-up and
face-only perspectives by cropping the original full-body
images.
The face-only perspective is obtained using the Reti-
naFace library [19], which provides a bounding box of the
face. This bounding box is directly used to crop the image to
the face-only perspective. To obtain the torso-up perspective,
we reuse the keypoint annotations obtained during the fil-
tering process, in particular the shoulder and eye keypoints.
Hence, the width of the crop is determined by the distance
between the shoulder x-coordinates, and the height of the
crop is determined by the distance between the y-coordinates
of the lowest shoulder and highest eye keypoints. To ensure
that the cropping contains the entire torso and head, a margin
is added to the crop. The size of the margin is determined
relative to the size of the crop and is set to 50% on both the
width and height of the crop.

3.3. Computer Vision Model
Model Architecture
Our work adopts the architecture proposed by Jin et
al. (2022) for BMI estimation from 2D body images [5].
The network is a DenseNet Convolutional Neural Net-
work (CNN) [20]. Jin et al. demonstrated that this architec-
ture outperforms other CNN architectures on the task of BMI
estimation from full-body images, including ResNet and
VGG architectures. Whereas Jin et al. used a DenseNet121
architecture, we use a DenseNet201 backbone to leverage
its increased capacity to learn more complex features from
larger datasets.
Attention Mechanism
A crucial enhancement to the base DenseNet architecture is
the addition of Squeeze and Excition (SE) blocks[21] after
each transition layer. These SE blocks effectively function as
an attention mechanism, allowing the model to focus on the
most informative features at each stage of the network. A sin-
gle SE block consists of a global average pooling layer that
aggregates the spatial information into a channel descriptor.
This descriptor is then passed through a ”squeeze” operation
using a 1×1 convolution to reduce the number of channels
(thereby decreasing computational complexity), followed
by a ReLU activation layer. The squeeze operation reduces
the input channel dimension (C) to a smaller ”bottleneck”
dimension (C/r), where r is a reduction ratio, a hyperparam-
eter. The reduction ratio is typically set to 16, as it has been
shown to provide a good trade-off between performance and
computational complexity [21].
Next, an ”excitation” step is performed using another 1×1
convolution to restore the channel dimension, after which a
sigmoid (or its approximation) normalizes the output to gen-
erate channel-wise weights. These weights are finally applied
multiplicatively to the original feature maps, enabling the
network to emphasize more informative channels while sup-
pressing less useful ones [21]. Jin et al. (2022) demonstrated
that the addition of SE blocks to a DenseNet architecture
significantly improved the performance of the model on the
task of BMI estimation [5].

Training details
We split the dataset into training, test, and validation sets of
75%, 15%, and 10% respectively. To ensure that the same
individual does not appear in multiple sets, we group the data
by user and randomly shuffle the user list. Then, for each
user, we calculate the remaining number of photos needed
in each partition and assign the user to the partition with the
largest gap. This way, all photos from a given user remain
together while the overall dataset stays balanced. For full
details, see the pseudocode in Figure 7 in the appendix.
We then train separate models for each perspective. The
base Densenet201 model is pre-trained on the ImageNet
dataset [22], however, we leave all layers trainable during
training. We then train each model for 40 epochs with a batch
size of 64, using the Adam optimizer [23] with a learning
rate of 0.001 and weight decay of 0.0001. We use the Mean
Squared Error (MSE) loss function to train the model. This
is in keeping with the hyperparameters and loss function
used by Jin et al. (2022) [5]. We track Mean Absolute Error
(MAE) and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for
each epoch but do not use these metrics to guide training. No
further hyperparameter tuning was performed. Additionally,
we dynamically reduce the learning rate by a factor of ‘0.1‘
when validation loss plateaus, with a patience of ‘5‘ epochs
to prevent overfitting and ensure convergence. All models
are trained using the PyTorch framework [24] on a single
NVIDIA T4 GPU.
4. Results
In this section, we present the results of our experiments.
First, we present details of our proprietary dataset in Sec-
tion 4.1. We describe the the results of the filtering process
applied to the dataset in Section4.2. Lastly, we present the
evaluation of the deep learning model evaluated on the differ-
ent image perspectives (full-body, torso-up, and face-only)
in Section 4.3. Additionally, we evaluate our model on three
external datasets, unseen during model training.
4.1. Dataset
The proprietary dataset consists of 84,963 photos of 25,353
individuals. Images were collected from users of a fitness
app over the course of 10+ years, with users using their own
smartphones (different Android and iOS devices through-
out the years) to capture the images. Over 900k individuals
shared their pictures through the weight loss app, resulting
in over 6 million images. Of these, 25,353 users provided
explicit consent for their images to be used in research, under
the condition that the images will not be publicly released
and cannot be inferred from any published results.
Subjects were instructed to take a front-facing photo of
themselves containing their full-body at various stages of
a fitness program for progress-tracking. They were asked

to submit a photo once in a while and also provide their
weight at the time of the photo. The height of each user was
self-reported at the beginning of the fitness program. Par-
ticipants in the fitness program were instructed to capture
front-facing, full-body images taken at a horizontal angle.
Most participants adhered to these guidelines, as confirmed
through human inspection of a subset of the dataset (random
samples). However, some uploads included non-human con-
tent—such as animals, selfies, or distorted images. We did
not assess the exact number of such invalid entries, but found
them solely by looking at rejected images of our filtering
pipeline.

4.2. Filtering
The filtering of the dataset resulted in 13.642 (16.2%) images
being removed before training. 12.402 images were removed
due to the bounding box being too small, 513 images were
removed due to a low confidence score for the bounding box,
and 2,052 images were removed due to unsuitable poses.
The various steps do not sum to the total number of removed
images, as filtering steps were applied independently and
some images met multiple exclusion criteria. Figure 4 shows
the distribution and overlap of images removed by each
filtering step.
Posture Clustering
The optimal number of clusters was determined to be 4 using
the elbow criterion (see Figure 9b). Inspecting the first two
clusters, we observed that they both corresponded to the most
common pose in the dataset: standing upright in a frontal
position. The difference between the two clusters was the
position of the arms, with one cluster having the arms by
the side and the other having one or both arms raised to
hold a camera. The third and fourth clusters consisted of
outlying postures, mostly involving pictures from alternative
camera angles. The latter two clusters were removed from
the dataset.

5. Discussion
In this Section, we discuss the practical implications of our
findings and highlight the limitations of our study.
Principal findings
Our model demonstrates strong gener-
alizability to unseen data, as demonstrated by our evaluation
on the full-body Visual-Body-To-BMI dataset, achieving a
MAPE of 13.38%, despite not being trained on this dataset
at all. Further, our results demonstrate that the full-body per-
spective yields the best overall performance, achieving the
lowest MAPE on BMI prediction (7.9%). This suggests that
the comprehensive spatial context—including body shape
and possibly background information—is crucial for accu-
rate weight estimation. Notably, the torso-up perspective
also performs well, with a MAPE of 9.1%. This indicates
that torso-up images may provide sufficient information for
accurate weight estimation, making them a viable alternative
in scenarios where full-body images are not available. The
face-only perspective yields the lowest performance, with a
MAPE of 11.1%, or an MAE of 3.66 BMI units and 10.38 kg.
These results are in the same range as the previous work that
has focused on facial images for weight estimation[7, 6, 15].
Comparison to prior work
To the best of our knowledge,
we present the first evaluation of a deep learning model for
BMI estimation on a large-scale, real-world dataset com-
prising 84,963 images - significantly exceeding the size of
datasets used in prior studies. For context, previous work
has relied on 14,500 facial images or just 5,900 full-body
images, as in the Visual-Body-To-BMI dataset [8].
Notably, this performance is comparable to that of the
original authors, who reported a MAPE of 12.50% [8] while
training on portions of the dataset and testing on the re-
maining parts. We want to highlight, that our model was
trained solely on the real-world dataset containing images
with highly variable quality, lighting, and posture conditions.
However, our model did not perform as well on the
face-only VIP Attribute dataset, where the original authors
achieved an MAE of 2.36 on body weight prediction, versus
our MAE of 7.81. We partly attribute this discrepancy to the
significant differences between the celebrity headshots in the
VIP attribute and the conditions of our training dataset. Ac-
cording to our findings, BMI estimation performs best with
full-body and torso images taken from a front-facing, stan-
dard pose—defined, i.e., with the subject standing upright,
facing the camera.
Moreover, while prior studies have typically focused on
either face-only or full-body images, our work is the first to
provide a direct comparison of different image perspectives
within a homogeneous dataset. On full-body images, our
model achieves a MAPE of 7.9%. To our knowledge, this is
the lowest reported MAPE for this task, outperforming the
9.6% MAPE reported by Jin et al. (2022) [5]. To the best of
our knowledge we present the first evaluation of a pre-trained
BMI estimation model on datasets entirely unseen during
training.
Our work also provides insights for remote weight esti-
mation during telemedicine consultations. In these scenarios,
patients may only be visible from the torso up. Our results
show that torso-up images provide performance comparable
to full-body images, suggesting that torso-up images may
be sufficient for accurate weight estimation in telemedicine
applications.
Practical Implications
Anyone interested in replicating
our approach can do so using the publicly available source
code we provide. We also provide the source code for the ap-
plication itself, enabling the deployment of our approach in
real-world scenarios. While we are unable to share the model
weights trained on our proprietary dataset—due to data pri-
vacy concerns and the potential risk of reverse-engineering
the original data—we encourage others to use our training
scripts to develop their own models on alternative datasets.
These models can be seamlessly deployed using our CLAID
package and the accompanying mobile applications for An-
droid and iOS. Additionally, the codebase includes our fil-
tering pipeline, which is used in the applications to give a
warning when an unsuitable picture is taken.
Limitations
Based on our experiments, we consider the
following limitations of our study:
1. Self-reported height and weight labels: The height and
weight labels in our dataset were self-reported by the
participants. This introduces the potential for inaccuracies
and biases in the data.
8

2. Gender imbalance: The training dataset has a significant
gender imbalance, with 49% female, 9% male, and 42%
not providing their gender. This imbalance could affect
the model’s performance across different genders.
3. Lack of hyperparameter search: We followed the hyper-
parameters used by Jin et al. (2022) [5] in their state-of-
the-art model. However, a more extensive hyperparameter
search could potentially improve the performance of our
model.

3. Methodology
In this section, we describe our approach to estimating BMI
of a person from real-world smartphone camera images. First,
we describe the filtering process we employ to remove un-
suitable images from the real-world dataset (cf. Section3.1).
We further describe cropping strategies to obtain different
image perspectives, i.e., full body, torso-up, and face-only
images (cf. Section 3.2). Lastly, we explain the implementa-
tion and training of the deep learning model used for BMI
estimation (cf. Section 3.3).
3.1. Image filtering
Images captured in real-life scenarios often exhibit signifi-
cant variation in factors such as image quality, lighting, and
subject posture. Some images - particularly those taken from
uncommon angles or with atypical postures - may be unsuit-
able for accurate BMI estimation. To ensure that we only
include suitable images into our dataset, we apply a filtering
process to automatically curate the real-world dataset. Our
goal is to remove images that do not (clearly) contain a hu-
man body, images with a camera angle that is too low or too
high (such as selfies), and images with outlying postures.
To identify outlier images, we apply a set of filtering steps
based on human bounding box and body keypoint data, both
obtained using the Detectron2 framework [18]. The Detec-
tron2 framework provides models for human bounding box
estimation, including confidence scores, as well as skeleton
estimation with 17 human body keypoints. Using bounding
pox and keypoint estimations, we apply three filtering steps:
1. Person detection: Images with a human bounding box
confidence score of less than a certain threshold are re-
moved
2. Person-to-background-ratio: Images with a bounding-
box-to-image-area-ratio below a certain threshold are
removed (see Figure 5 in the results for an example)
3. Posture clustering: images with outlying combinations of
body keypoints were clustered and removed (details in
the below subsection)
Each filtering step is applied independently, and the images
that meet any of the conditions are removed from the dataset.
We note, that it is possible for one image to meet multiple
filtering conditions at once.
Posture clustering
Participants received instructions to have another person
take their picture from a distance in a front-facing, full-
body position. Visual inspection of our dataset confirms that
most participants followed these instructions and maintained
suitable postures. Given that most people uploaded good
pictures, we apply k-means clustering to the extracted pose
keypoints to distinguish suitable postures from outliers. This
clustering allows us to filter out images where the subject
displays unsuitable poses - such as twisted arms or legs -or
where the photo was taken from an elevated angle, such as
selfies.
To ensures that the clustering is based on the relative po-
sition of the keypoints rather than the absolute position (i.e.,
given different sizes and positions of each person in the pic-
ture), we normalize the coordinates of the body keypoints by
dividing them by the individual image width and height. This
also allows us the plot the keypoints on a common scale for
visual inspection. For each image, we have a set of 34 nor-
malized coordinates (17 keypoints with x and y coordinates).
Since not all keypoints provide discriminative information,
we apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce
the dimensionality of the data. We remove components as
many as long as we retain 95% of the variance in the data.
We then apply K-means clustering to the dimensionality-
reduced dataset of keypoint coordinates. We evaluate k=1
to k=10 clusters. Using the elbow method, we determine
the optimal number of clusters. Afterwards, using visual in-
spection, we determine which clusters correspond to useable
poses. The other clusters are removed from the dataset.
3.2. Perspective cropping
We consider three perspectives: full-body, torso-up, and face-
only. The full-body perspective contains the entire body of
the individual, the torso-up perspective contains the body
from the shoulders up, and the face-only perspective contains
only the face of the individual. We obtain the torso-up and
face-only perspectives by cropping the original full-body
images.
The face-only perspective is obtained using the Reti-
naFace library [19], which provides a bounding box of the
face. This bounding box is directly used to crop the image to
the face-only perspective. To obtain the torso-up perspective,
we reuse the keypoint annotations obtained during the fil-
tering process, in particular the shoulder and eye keypoints.
Hence, the width of the crop is determined by the distance
between the shoulder x-coordinates, and the height of the
crop is determined by the distance between the y-coordinates
of the lowest shoulder and highest eye keypoints. To ensure
that the cropping contains the entire torso and head, a margin
is added to the crop. The size of the margin is determined
relative to the size of the crop and is set to 50% on both the
width and height of the crop.

3.3. Computer Vision Model
Model Architecture
Our work adopts the architecture proposed by Jin et
al. (2022) for BMI estimation from 2D body images [5].
The network is a DenseNet Convolutional Neural Net-
work (CNN) [20]. Jin et al. demonstrated that this architec-
ture outperforms other CNN architectures on the task of BMI
estimation from full-body images, including ResNet and
VGG architectures. Whereas Jin et al. used a DenseNet121
architecture, we use a DenseNet201 backbone to leverage
its increased capacity to learn more complex features from
larger datasets.
Attention Mechanism
A crucial enhancement to the base DenseNet architecture is
the addition of Squeeze and Excition (SE) blocks[21] after
each transition layer. These SE blocks effectively function as
an attention mechanism, allowing the model to focus on the
most informative features at each stage of the network. A sin-
gle SE block consists of a global average pooling layer that
aggregates the spatial information into a channel descriptor.
This descriptor is then passed through a ”squeeze” operation
using a 1×1 convolution to reduce the number of channels
(thereby decreasing computational complexity), followed
by a ReLU activation layer. The squeeze operation reduces
the input channel dimension (C) to a smaller ”bottleneck”
dimension (C/r), where r is a reduction ratio, a hyperparam-
eter. The reduction ratio is typically set to 16, as it has been
shown to provide a good trade-off between performance and
computational complexity [21].
Next, an ”excitation” step is performed using another 1×1
convolution to restore the channel dimension, after which a
sigmoid (or its approximation) normalizes the output to gen-
erate channel-wise weights. These weights are finally applied
multiplicatively to the original feature maps, enabling the
network to emphasize more informative channels while sup-
pressing less useful ones [21]. Jin et al. (2022) demonstrated
that the addition of SE blocks to a DenseNet architecture
significantly improved the performance of the model on the
task of BMI estimation [5].

We split the dataset into training, test, and validation sets of
75%, 15%, and 10% respectively. To ensure that the same
individual does not appear in multiple sets, we group the data
by user and randomly shuffle the user list. Then, for each
user, we calculate the remaining number of photos needed
in each partition and assign the user to the partition with the
largest gap. This way, all photos from a given user remain
together while the overall dataset stays balanced. For full
details, see the pseudocode in Figure 7 in the appendix.
We then train separate models for each perspective. The
base Densenet201 model is pre-trained on the ImageNet
dataset [22], however, we leave all layers trainable during
training. We then train each model for 40 epochs with a batch
size of 64, using the Adam optimizer [23] with a learning
rate of 0.001 and weight decay of 0.0001. We use the Mean
Squared Error (MSE) loss function to train the model. This
is in keeping with the hyperparameters and loss function
used by Jin et al. (2022) [5]. We track Mean Absolute Error
(MAE) and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) for
each epoch but do not use these metrics to guide training. No
further hyperparameter tuning was performed. Additionally,
we dynamically reduce the learning rate by a factor of ‘0.1‘
when validation loss plateaus, with a patience of ‘5‘ epochs
to prevent overfitting and ensure convergence. All models
are trained using the PyTorch framework [24] on a single
NVIDIA T4 GPU.
4. Results
In this section, we present the results of our experiments.
First, we present details of our proprietary dataset in Sec-
tion 4.1. We describe the the results of the filtering process
applied to the dataset in Section4.2. Lastly, we present the
evaluation of the deep learning model evaluated on the differ-
ent image perspectives (full-body, torso-up, and face-only)
in Section 4.3. Additionally, we evaluate our model on three
external datasets, unseen during model training.
4.1. Dataset
The proprietary dataset consists of 84,963 photos of 25,353
individuals. Images were collected from users of a fitness
app over the course of 10+ years, with users using their own
smartphones (different Android and iOS devices through-
out the years) to capture the images. Over 900k individuals
shared their pictures through the weight loss app, resulting
in over 6 million images. Of these, 25,353 users provided
explicit consent for their images to be used in research, under
the condition that the images will not be publicly released
and cannot be inferred from any published results.
Subjects were instructed to take a front-facing photo of
themselves containing their full-body at various stages of
a fitness program for progress-tracking. They were asked
4.1. Dataset

to submit a photo once in a while and also provide their
weight at the time of the photo. The height of each user was
self-reported at the beginning of the fitness program. Par-
ticipants in the fitness program were instructed to capture
front-facing, full-body images taken at a horizontal angle.
Most participants adhered to these guidelines, as confirmed
through human inspection of a subset of the dataset (random
samples). However, some uploads included non-human con-
tent—such as animals, selfies, or distorted images. We did
not assess the exact number of such invalid entries, but found
them solely by looking at rejected images of our filtering
pipeline.
49% of the subjects in the dataset are female and 9% are
male, with the remaining 42% not providing their gender.

4.2. Filtering
The filtering of the dataset resulted in 13.642 (16.2%) images
being removed before training. 12.402 images were removed
due to the bounding box being too small, 513 images were
removed due to a low confidence score for the bounding box,
and 2,052 images were removed due to unsuitable poses.
The various steps do not sum to the total number of removed
images, as filtering steps were applied independently and
some images met multiple exclusion criteria. Figure 4 shows
the distribution and overlap of images removed by each
filtering step.
Posture Clustering
The optimal number of clusters was determined to be 4 using
the elbow criterion (see Figure 9b). Inspecting the first two
clusters, we observed that they both corresponded to the most
common pose in the dataset: standing upright in a frontal
position. The difference between the two clusters was the
position of the arms, with one cluster having the arms by
the side and the other having one or both arms raised to
hold a camera. The third and fourth clusters consisted of
outlying postures, mostly involving pictures from alternative
camera angles. The latter two clusters were removed from
the dataset.

Practical Implications
Anyone interested in replicating
our approach can do so using the publicly available source
code we provide. We also provide the source code for the ap-
plication itself, enabling the deployment of our approach in
real-world scenarios. While we are unable to share the model
weights trained on our proprietary dataset—due to data pri-
vacy concerns and the potential risk of reverse-engineering
the original data—we encourage others to use our training
scripts to develop their own models on alternative datasets.
These models can be seamlessly deployed using our CLAID
package and the accompanying mobile applications for An-
droid and iOS. Additionally, the codebase includes our fil-
tering pipeline, which is used in the applications to give a
warning when an unsuitable picture is taken.
Limitations
Based on our experiments, we consider the
following limitations of our study:
1. Self-reported height and weight labels: The height and
weight labels in our dataset were self-reported by the
participants. This introduces the potential for inaccuracies
and biases in the data.
8

2. Gender imbalance: The training dataset has a significant
gender imbalance, with 49% female, 9% male, and 42%
not providing their gender. This imbalance could affect
the model’s performance across different genders.
3. Lack of hyperparameter search: We followed the hyper-
parameters used by Jin et al. (2022) [5] in their state-of-
the-art model. However, a more extensive hyperparameter
search could potentially improve the performance of our
model.
Code and Data Availability. The code used for this study
is available at https://github.com/RealLast/
DigitalScale. The dataset used is proprietary and not
publicly available. Any example images shown in this paper
are for illustrative purposes only, taken from the Visual-
Body-to-BMI dataset. No images taken from the proprietary
dataset are shown in this paper.
